back: The encoder reads the source; the decoder, initialised from the encoder state (or attending to it), emits target tokens one by one: a conditional LM $P(y_t\mid y_{<t},x)$.
Greedy takes the arg max token at each step; beam search keeps the B best partial outputs (B around 4-5 in translation).
Each candidate n-gram is counted at most as often as its maximum count in any reference.
$1$ if $|c|>\rho$, else $e^{1-\rho/|c|}$; $\rho$ is the closest reference length. Stands in for recall.
Any zero n-gram precision gives 0; BLEU is designed for corpora (or needs smoothing).
n-gram overlap (clipped) reported as precision, recall and F1; recall-oriented, standard for summaries.
Uses the longest common subsequence (in order, not necessarily adjacent); DP in $O(|c||r|)$.
Extractive selects source sentences (faithful, rigid). Abstractive generates new text (fluent, can hallucinate).
Encode question+passage, score each token as start and end; pick $i\le j<i+L_{max}$ maximising $s_i+e_j$.
After normalising (lowercase, no punctuation or articles): EM requires equal strings; F1 uses bag-of-token overlap.
Retriever finds passages, reader extracts or generates the answer: the basis of RAG.
They measure surface similarity, not meaning: paraphrases score low, fluent errors can score high; compare with baselines and humans.
Standard tokenisation and a signature make BLEU scores reproducible and comparable.
